newsitem.title: UK: Marks & Spencer profits hit record, adds 1,700 jobs.
newsitem.headline: Marks & Spencer profits hit record, adds 1,700 jobs.

text.p: Marks and Spencer Plc, Britain's biggest clothing retailer, Tuesday reported record profits for 1996 and unveiled an aggressive $2.5 billion expansion plan that it said would create 1,700 new jobs in Britain.
The company also said profits at its Brooks Brothers chain based in New York, jumped 62 percent for the year as sales rose 12.5 percent.

Chairman Richard Greenbury said the company, which has stores in Europe, North America and Asia, had increased its share of clothing sales in Britain and held steady in food sales despite fierce competition.
"It's a very, very competitive environment in clothing, in foods, in retailing generally. In every single area it's competitive," he said in an interview.

Pretax profits rose about 14 percent to 1.1 billion pounds ($1.8 billion) in the year ended on March 31, from 966 million ($1.6 billion) a year earlier. Sales grew 8 percent to 7.8 billion pounds ($12.9 billion) from 7.2 billion ($11.8 billion).

Brooks Brothers, including operations in Japan, had operating profits of $26.9 million, up from $16.6 million a year earlier. Sales grew to $523 million from $465 million and sales at stores open at least a year grew 10 percent.
Industry analysts said Marks & Spencer was emerging as a winner as department store retailers and food superstores wage a fierce battle to lure customers.
The retailer plans to spend the bulk of the 1.5 billion pounds ($2.5 billion) earmarked for expansion in Britain and continental Europe, including 30 or 40 sites in Germany, France and Spain.
Greenbury said there were still opportunities to expand in Britain even though the company was in many town centres and in suburbs.

He said additional staff would not mean costs would rise faster than sales. He also said he was not worried about the new Labour government's plans for a minimum wage, since Marks & Spencer paid staff more than the minimum being talked about.
"Whatever happens ... if you include both the bonus at Christmas and the non-contributory pension, we're paying over 6 pounds ($9.85) an hour."
Overseas businesses including Brooks Brothers did well despite the strong pound as operating profits rose 23 percent and sales grew 9 percent.

The company said next year profits would be reduced by 20 million pounds ($33 million) because of the strength of the pound, which erodes sales in other countries when they are converted back into pounds.
It also plans to expand mail order and will begin a regional trial of clothing catalogues next year.
